analysis: Examined the two base_text excerpts of fixtures/prompt-contract/v1/production_vectors.json (base lines 23289-25220). These are gemma-4-26b-8bit and gemma-4-26b-qat-4bit test vectors: tool_call_arguments_bridge, tool_function_extra_keys, tools, unicode, assistant_harmony_framing, endpoint_* cases. They contain request_body, provider_body, template_input, plan block boundaries and token_ids. The patch excerpt is truncated; it shows a Qwen-style vector change (added additional_context enable_thinking=false, token count 803->767, changed chain hashes, removed 768-token block). No runtime code, authorization, attestation, key custody, or WebSocket/App Attest logic is changed in the supplied evidence. The fixtures contain only synthetic data (fixture-scope, example prompts, no secrets or credentials). The security-relevant link is the prompt-contract/cache-block chain hashes consumed by the encrypted prefix-cache threat T-041 (cross-tenant cache sharing and TTFT oracle). A change to block boundaries or chain hashes alters cache-key derivation in test vectors. Whether the matching Swift/Go implementation preserves scope isolation (scope_id) cannot be verified from fixtures alone. Remaining integration questions: confirm the implementation change producing the new vectors (additional_context and the chat-template change) does not weaken scope_id binding in chain hashes or the contract id, and that the Go and Swift sides both consume the updated vectors. The base-side excerpts I saw are mostly unchanged context. The changed ranges are elsewhere in the file and are only partly visible in the truncated patch. No concrete regression is identified from these units.
